title: Woe that day
hookLine: the refrain repeated ten times: woe that day to the deniers (77:15)

cards: Some songs are built on a chorus. The verse changes, the story moves, and then the same line comes back, and by the third time you're waiting for it.
Earlier this year, ar-Rahman did that with a question: which of your Lord's favors will you deny? Al-Mursalat does it too, with a shorter line and a heavier one.
It comes back ten times in fifty verses, and the whole surah is built around it.

teach.b: Surah seventy-seven, verse fifteen, in Pickthall's translation: "Woe unto the repudiators on that day!" In Arabic, waylun yawma'idhin lil-mukadhdhibin. Wayl is woe, a cry of ruin.
Yawma'idhin, on that day, the Day the surah has been describing. And al-mukadhdhibin comes from the root k-dh-b, to lie.

The form here means more than people who doubt: it's people who call a true thing a lie, who look at it and say, that's false. Pickthall's old word, repudiators, catches that: people who disown what's in front of them.
Now watch where the refrain falls. It doesn't only follow scenes of the end.
Again and again it follows a gift. Did We not create you from a humble fluid, and shape you? Woe that day to the deniers.

Did We not make the earth a place that holds the living and the dead, set firm mountains on it, and give you sweet water to drink? Woe that day to the deniers. The warning keeps landing right after something good.
Some commentators read it that way: the denial in view isn't only of the Day, but of the gifts that point to it. To be handed water, a body, solid ground, and call the giver a fiction.
So the refrain works in two directions: a warning about the end, and a nudge about this afternoon.

teach.h: WHAT GOOD AM I CALLING NOTHING?
teach.b: What good thing in front of you have you been quietly treating as nothing?

how: Al-Mursalat is recited in prayer and in personal reading; its refrain returns ten times, and commentators read each return against the sign that comes just before it.

o: the deniers, who call a true thing a lie
the messengers sent to warn every nation
the doubters who are still asking honestly

games.q: woe that day — tap the pairs.
p: the root: to lie, to call a lie
how often the refrain comes back

s: the refrain only follows scenes of the end
it often follows a gift: the body, the earth, sweet water.
mukadhdhibin means people who call a true thing a lie
from k-dh-b, to lie: Pickthall says repudiators.
ar-Rahman's refrain and al-Mursalat's are the same line
ar-Rahman asks which favors you will deny; al-Mursalat warns of woe that day.

games.q: the surah asks: did We not create you from a humble fluid, and shape you? what line comes right after?
o: woe that day to the deniers.
games.why: the refrain. it lands right after a gift, which is how some commentators read it: the denial is of gifts as well as of the Day.

practice: Look back over the last day for one good thing you brushed off: a compliment you waved away, a meal someone made that you ate standing up, a morning you woke up healthy and didn't notice.
Hold it for a moment without arguing with it, and let it be what it was: a good thing, given.

wordCard.voice: Al-mukadhdhibin. Woe that day to the deniers, said ten times in al-Mursalat, often right after a gift: water, body, ground. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 77:15: woe that day to the deniers.

carryVoice: Your line: don't deny it. The refrain keeps falling right after the gifts. That's day six hundred sixty-three.

sources.q: Woe unto the repudiators on that day!
